extracted.intended_audience: HCI and software-engineering researchers and practitioners interested in code review, feedback, and inclusion
extracted.subtask_short: survey study on code review criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A mixed-methods survey and vignette study measuring perceptions, frequency, impact, and responses to constructive vs destructive code review feedback among software developers. Includes quantitative models and thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destructive criticism dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions distinguished between nonspecific negative feedback and inconsiderate negative feedback, which are the two main aspects of destructive criticism [10].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat destructive criticism as composed of (1) nonspecific negative feedback (negative but not actionable) and (2) inconsiderate negative feedback (rude/insulting tone). Use both aspects when measuring frequency and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception measures (vignette items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants rated agreement that the feedback would help improve the code, was valid, and was appropriate (vignette questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Likert-scale items for each perception: e.g., 'This feedback would help me to improve the code', 'This feedback is valid', 'This feedback is appropriate'. For analysis convert Likert responses to integers from -2 (strongly disagree / very unmotivated) to +2 (strongly agree / very motivated) when computing averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on motivation measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivation measures asked: 'How motivated do you think you would be to: Continue working on this task?', 'Continue working with this developer?', and 'Continue working on this project?' in regard to the vignette feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare responses for constructive vs destructive feedback; expect destructive feedback to reduce motivation across these three dimensions. Use ordinal analysis on Likert responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mood items
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants reported perceived mood after receiving feedback using categories: Great, At ease, Good, Composed, Bad, Tense, Nervous, Uncomfortable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report prevalence of positive vs negative moods for constructive vs destructive feedback; use Chi-squared tests for association (example: negative moods much higher under destructive feedback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency measurement conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency questions distinguished how often participants gave/received feedback with categories such as once or more a year, once or more a quarter, once or more a month, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure frequency separately for nonspecific and inconsiderate destructive feedback. Use these frequency measures as independent variables in regression models when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response-type taxonomy for written replies
rubrics_metrics.description: Five types of written responses were identified: Ask for more information; Agree with the criticism; Disagree with the criticism on a technical level; Disagree with the manner of discourse; Acknowledge comment reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing open-ended replies, code responses into these categories (allow multiple theme assignments per response when applicable). Note which types are more associated with destructive vs constructive feedback (e.g., 'Ask for more information' more common for destructive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-response tone categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Six tones were used to categorize responses: Neutral; Gratitude; Apology; Praise; Sarcasm; Anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign a single dominant tone per response. Expect gratitude/praise more for constructive feedback; sarcasm/anger/apology more for destructive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression model independent variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent variables in regression models: gender (categorical: man, woman, non-binary); highest education level (categorical: less than undergraduate, undergraduate, postgraduate); experience in years (numeric); self-efficacy score (numeric, average across eight self-efficacy questions); self-reported competence (categorical: low/average, moderately high, high); has contributed to one or more OSS projects (binary); is a student (binary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include frequency of giving/receiving feedback as independent variables when modeling frequency outcomes. Combine low-count categories (e.g., high school + some undergraduate; low + average competence) to avoid sparse cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal logistic regression was used since dependent variables were responses to Likert-scale questions (ordered categorical). In one case (frequency of inconsiderate feedback received), ordinal logistic regression was not suitable due to non-normally distributed dependent variable and a log-log model was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select model form appropriate to the dependent variable distribution. Check model fit and consider alternative link functions if assumptions violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multicollinearity and variable exclusion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Age was excluded from the models because it was highly correlated with years of experience (Pearson correlation 0.84). Variance inflation factors (VIF) for independent variables were computed and showed no multicollinearity issues (Table 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute VIFs and exclude highly collinear predictors (prefer precise measures such as exact years of experience over correlated brackets like age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness-of-fit and significance reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness-of-fit was measured using the Pulkstenis-Robinson chi-squared test with the 'generalhoslem' R package. When reporting regression results, significant results are bolded and asterisks denote p-values: * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001. Model coefficients are reported in 'Value' columns and standard errors in 'SE' columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Pulkstenis-Robinson for categorical dependent-variable models; clearly mark significance with asterisk conventions and report coefficients with standard errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect-size interpretation (Cohen's d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect sizes were calculated using Cohen’s D. With this measure, d<0.2 is considered a negligible effect, d>=0.2 is considered a small effect, d>=0.5 is considered a medium effect, and d>=0.8 is considered a large effect [25].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Cohen's D for group mean differences and interpret using these thresholds. Example: large negative d for destructive vs constructive on perceived appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic analysis protocol for open-ended responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Thematic Analysis was performed independently by two authors who coded all responses. Final themes were developed through iterative discussions between those two authors and regular discussions with a third author. Conflicts were discussed until consensus was reached. This analysis was performed without knowledge of who made the comment and their reported demographic information; demographics were examined only after themes were finalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use independent coders, iterative discussion with an adjudicator, blind coding to demographics to avoid bias, then qualitatively examine demographic trends post-coding. Use median-split on experience (median = 5 years) to define 'more' vs 'less' experienced for qualitative trend inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical guidance for writing code review comments
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked which is most important: 'Feedback that will improve code quality'; 'Feedback that will not cause a negative reaction for the code author'; 'Both are equally important' — most participants (67 of 88, 76%) responded that both improving code quality and preventing a negative reaction are equally important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to provide comments that both improve code quality and avoid causing negative reactions. Provide detailed, considerate explanations rather than nonspecific or purely negative remarks. Recognize that some developers prefer direct wording, but balance directness with actionable detail and politeness.
